analysis.one_liner: Bans the President, Vice President, and members of Congress and their families from owning or trading individual stocks and digital assets.
analysis.headline: A Senate committee advanced a bill barring members of Congress, the President, and the Vice President and their families from owning individual stocks or crypto, with 5 cosponsors from both parties; the full Senate has not voted.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban members of Congress, the President, and the Vice President — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying or selling individual stocks, digital assets, and similar investments while in office and for 90 days after leaving. They would have to divest what they hold (diversified funds, Treasury bonds, and certain other holdings are allowed) and could no longer hide stock in qualified blind trusts. It also requires officials to report federal loans or grants their family businesses receive, forces financial disclosures into a searchable online database, and adds a $500 fine for late stock-trade reports.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who currently cannot know whether the people writing laws are betting on the companies those laws affect. The bill would remove the financial conflicts of interest of the most powerful federal officials, force divestment of individual stocks and crypto, publish family trust requests and divestiture notices online in searchable form, and fine officials $500 for late trade reports. Officials who own no individual stocks also benefit by no longer facing suspicion.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters; honest public trust in Congress

how_it_helps.text: Bars members of Congress, the President, and the Vice President, plus their spouses and dependent children, from purchasing or selling individual stocks, commodities, futures, or digital assets, with violations carrying civil penalties of the greater of a month's pay or 10% of the undisclosed holding's value every 30 days.

Forces officials to divest existing holdings, including those parked in qualified blind trusts, which the bill phases out as a hiding place, and covers indirectly held interests through funds, holding companies, trusts, and carried-interest arrangements.
Keeps the ban in place for 90 days after an official leaves office, closing the exit-window in which officials could trade on knowledge from their last weeks in power.

Requires ethics offices to post divestiture notices, family trust requests and responses, and any federal loans, grants, or benefits received by officials or their family businesses on a searchable public website, and makes all congressional financial disclosure forms searchable, sortable, and machine-readable online.
Adds an automatic $500 fine for every late stock-transaction report under the existing STOCK Act, addressing the current lack of any penalty for filing late.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, the President, and the Vice President and their families, who would have to sell individual stocks and digital assets and keep their money in diversified funds, Treasury securities, corporate bonds, or other allowed holdings. The public pays a small administrative cost for the ethics offices and the searchable disclosure databases; divestitures get tax-deferral treatment so officials are not hit with surprise capital-gains bills.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress, the President, and their families

drawbacks.text: Enforcement is left to the House and Senate ethics committees — bodies made up of the very members being policed — and a member fined under the bill can appeal the fine to a vote on the floor of their own chamber, so members of Congress remain the final judges of each other's compliance.

The carve-outs are wide enough to matter: spouses may keep stock issued as compensation from their own job or corporate board service, officials may keep corporate bonds they already held on enactment day, small-business and family-farm interests can be exempted by the ethics office, and family trusts can win exemptions if the official did not fund them — each a channel a well-advised official could use.
The bill covers only the President, Vice President, and members of Congress, not other executive branch officials who hold comparable market-moving power.

The costs fall on the officials themselves are real: forced divestment of concentrated holdings and a 90-day post-service ban limit how officials manage their own wealth, which is why the bill includes tax deferral and extension processes to soften the burden.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — lawmakers and the two most powerful executive officials no longer able to hold or trade the very stocks their decisions move — goes to the public at almost no cost to anyone else. The bill's weaknesses are in design, not cost: it lets Congress's own ethics committees enforce it, lets a fined member appeal to a full floor vote of peers, and leaves several compensation and family-trust carve-outs. It is a genuine restriction, but its strength depends entirely on the ethics bodies it charges with enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate homeland security committee approved the bill and put it on the Senate's waiting list for floor action in December 2025, but the full Senate has not voted and no vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced the bill on April 28, 2025, originally titled the PELOSI Act, with five cosponsors — one Republican and four Democrats — and it was sent to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.
On July 30, 2025, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, meaning it approved an overhauled version.

On December 10, 2025, the committee, chaired by Senator Rand Paul, formally reported the rewritten bill — renamed the HONEST Act — which expanded the original version to cover the President and Vice President, digital assets, blind trusts, and federal payments to officials' family businesses.

The same day the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 294), the waiting list for floor action; no senator has voted on it and no floor vote has been scheduled.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress, the President, and the Vice President are better off so far: the bill restricting their stock trading has cleared committee but not reached a vote, so the current rules that allow them to hold and trade individual stocks remain in effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress, who can still trade stocks

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator sponsored the bill and one more Republican joined four Democratic cosponsors, and the Republican-chaired committee reported it favorably; no floor vote has occurred, so no party split in voting exists yet.

industries.industry: Incumbent federal officeholders (members of Congress, the President, and the Vice President and their families)
industries.note: The people the bill regulates are the concentrated interest it restrains: they would have to sell individual stocks, crypto, and blind-trust holdings and could not buy new ones in office or for 90 days after. Their interest in keeping the current rules runs directly against the transparency the bill offers voters.

The bill adds digital assets to the list of investments covered officials cannot hold, removing a small but influential class of politically connected holders; the effect on the industry itself is minor, and the rule mainly serves government integrity rather than targeting the industry.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has cleared committee and sits on the Senate calendar, which is further than most stock-trading ban proposals have gotten. But placement on the calendar does not guarantee a vote — the Majority Leader must schedule floor time, and similar bipartisan stock-trading bans have repeatedly died without one. With bipartisan sponsorship and a favorable committee report, a floor vote is possible in the remaining session, but if the Senate leadership never schedules it, the bill will expire with the 119th Congress in January 2027.
